content: Infantile esotropia (IE) is a condition characterized by the inward deviation of one or both eyes. The optimal approach to managing this condition, including the most effective type of intervention and the ideal timing for treatment, remains unclear. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and timing of both surgical and non-surgical treatments for IE, with the goal of improving ocular alignment and promoting the development of binocular single vision. A comprehensive search of multiple databases and trial registries was conducted in November 2021, without restrictions on date or language. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized trials comparing surgical and non-surgical interventions for IE. Standard Cochrane methodology was used to analyze the data, and the certainty of evidence for six outcomes was assessed using the GRADE system. Two studies involving a total of 234 children with IE were included in the review. The first study, conducted in South Africa between 2015 and 2018, enrolled 110 children with large-angle IE (≥ 40 prism diopters) and onset of esotropia before six months of age. This study compared up to three botulinum toxin injections with surgical intervention involving bimedial rectus muscle recession. Children were followed for six months. The study had significant limitations in design and implementation, leading to a high risk of bias or concerns in most domains. The results suggested that surgery might increase the likelihood of treatment success, defined as achieving orthophoria or residual esotropia of ≤ 10 prism diopters, compared to botulinum toxin injections. However, the evidence was very uncertain (risk ratio [RR] 1.88, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.27 to 2.77; 1 study, 101 participants; very low-certainty evidence). It is important to interpret these findings cautiously, as 23 children in the surgery group with baseline deviations > 60 prism diopters also received botulinum toxin during surgery to enhance the effect of the muscle recession. There was no significant difference between surgery and botulinum toxin injections in terms of over-correction (deviation > 10 prism diopters) (RR 0.29, 95% CI 0.06 to 1.37; 1 study, 101 participants; very low-certainty evidence) or the need for additional interventions (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.19; 1 study, 101 participants; very low-certainty evidence). No major surgical complications were reported in the surgery group. However, children in the botulinum toxin group experienced several complications, including partial transient ptosis in 16.7% of cases, transient vertical deviation in 5.6%, and consecutive exotropia in 24.1%. No other prespecified outcomes were reported in this study. The second study, conducted in 12 university hospitals in Germany and the Netherlands, enrolled 124 children with onset of esotropia before one year of age. This study compared bilateral rectus muscle recession with unilateral rectus muscle recession surgeries and followed children for three months postoperatively. The evidence, which was of very low certainty, suggested no significant difference between bilateral and unilateral surgeries in terms of achieving binocular vision (specific numbers not reported, P = 0.35) or the risk of over-correction (RR for exotropia 1.09, 95% CI 0.45 to 2.63; 1 study, 118 participants). Dissociated vertical deviation, latent nystagmus, or both were observed in 8% to 21% of participants. In conclusion, medial rectus muscle recession surgery may increase the likelihood of treatment success compared to botulinum toxin injections alone, but the evidence is very uncertain. No significant differences were found between bilateral and unilateral surgeries. Due to the limited and low-quality evidence available, this review was unable to resolve the controversies surrounding the type of surgery, non-surgical interventions, or the optimal age for intervention in IE. High-quality clinical trials are urgently needed to strengthen the evidence base for managing this condition.
